topic: firing a home-built brick bread oven and baking sourdough loaves in the stored heat

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-3)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: termometr piecowy zawieszony przy wylocie

base: I built a brick bread oven in the garden and fired it for the first time.
The village bakery still uses a much larger oven of the same old pattern.
I hung an oven thermometer inside the door, since the old spit-and-count method failed me.
My first loaves came out pale on top and burnt black underneath.
Should I fire the oven longer, or wait after raking the embers out?
Wait after raking, because a freshly cleared hearth is far hotter than the vault above.
The bricks need an hour to even out before any bread goes in.
Heat stored in the floor must travel upward into the crown of the oven.
Bread put in too soon always burns below and stays raw on top.
I raked the embers out and left the oven closed for a full hour.
The oven thermometer settled at two hundred and forty degrees before I loaded.
The loaves rose well but the crust stayed thin and rather too pale.
Is that a heat problem, or does my sourdough need something else?
That is steam, since a sealed oven holds the moisture that makes a crust shine.
Two hundred and forty degrees is ample heat for a hearth loaf.
Throw a cupful of water onto the floor as you close the door.
Seal the mouth with a wet cloth and let no steam escape early.
I threw water in and sealed the mouth, and the crust came out glossy.
The oven thermometer dropped only ten degrees across the whole of the bake.
The village oven turns out loaves with a much darker crust than mine.
Is that longer baking, or does their dough differ from mine somehow?
That is a longer, slower ferment, which builds the sugars that colour a crust.
A dough retarded overnight in the cold bakes far darker than a warm one.
Their loaves probably sit twelve hours before ever reaching the oven mouth.
Try mixing your dough in the evening and baking it the following morning instead.
I mixed the dough at eight and left it in the cold pantry.
By morning it had risen well and smelled far more strongly of acid.
The baked loaves are darker now but the crumb has turned rather dense.
Did I overproof the dough, or is my starter simply too sour?
You overproofed it slightly, because a cold pantry in summer is warmer than you assume.
Dough that goes too far loses the gas it needs for an open crumb.
Shape the loaves at midnight instead, and let them prove in a basket.
A shaped loaf holds its structure far better than one left in bulk.
I shaped the loaves at midnight and proved them in floured baskets overnight.
The crumb is open and the crust is dark and blistered all over.
Neighbours have started asking whether I would bake for them as well.
Can one firing handle enough loaves for a dozen households at once?
One firing will bake three batches, each cooler than the one before it.
Put the crusty loaves in first and the softer ones in afterwards.
The last of the heat will do pies, biscuits and slow puddings nicely.
Old ovens were always worked that way, from the fiercest bake to the gentlest.
